lesson.title: Is the Slope Real, or Just Noise?
lesson.summary: The sample slope b1 from a least-squares line estimates the true population slope, and a t-procedure with n minus 2 degrees of freedom tests whether that estimate reflects a real relationship or ordinary sampling variation.
lesson.body:
A least squares regression line, y-hat equals b0 plus b1 x, is built from one particular sample. Collect a different random sample from the same population or process, and you would very likely get a slightly different slope, b1. That variability is exactly the kind of problem statistical inference exists to handle: b1 is a statistic, computed from data, that estimates some true, fixed, unknown parameter, call it beta1, describing the actual linear relationship in the population or process being studied. The central question of slope inference is whether an observed b1 reflects a real relationship or could plausibly be explained by ordinary sample to sample variation around a true slope of zero.

The tool for answering that question is a t-procedure, structurally identical to other inference procedures you have used: a test statistic of the form statistic minus hypothesized parameter, divided by standard error, referred to a t-distribution, this time with n minus 2 degrees of freedom, two fewer than the sample size because two quantities, an intercept and a slope, were already estimated from the data in order to draw the line in the first place.

Here is a full worked example. Six students report hours studied, x, and their quiz score, y: (1,3), (2,5), (3,4), (4,8), (5,7), (6,9). Running the least squares calculations gives a slope b1 equals 8 over 7, approximately 1.143, and an intercept b0 equals 2, so the fitted line is y-hat equals 2 plus 1.143x. The residual standard deviation, how far actual scores typically fall from this fitted line, works out to about 1.134, and with the x-values spread out enough to give a sum of squared deviations of 17.5, the standard error of the slope is SE(b1) equals 1.134 divided by the square root of 17.5, approximately 0.271. In practice this standard error is read straight from computer or calculator regression output rather than computed by hand, but seeing where it comes from, residual spread divided by how spread out the x-values are, helps explain why a wider range of x-values or a tighter fit around the line both shrink SE(b1) and sharpen the inference.

Test the hypotheses H0: beta1 equals 0, no true linear relationship between hours studied and quiz score, against Ha: beta1 does not equal 0, some true linear relationship exists. The test statistic is t equals b1 minus 0, divided by SE(b1), equals 1.143 divided by 0.271, approximately 4.22, with df equals 6 minus 2 equals 4. A t-statistic of 4.22 on 4 degrees of freedom is quite extreme, producing a two-sided P-value of about 0.014. Since 0.014 is less than a standard alpha of 0.05, we reject H0: these six data points give convincing evidence of a real linear relationship between hours studied and quiz score.

The same standard error also builds a confidence interval for beta1, an equally valid way to summarize the same evidence: b1 plus or minus t-star times SE(b1), using the critical value for 4 degrees of freedom at 95% confidence, t-star equals 2.776. That gives 1.143 plus or minus 2.776 times 0.271, or 1.143 plus or minus about 0.752, an interval running from roughly 0.39 to 1.90. Notice how wide that interval is for such a small sample, a reminder that n equals 6 is really too small for a trustworthy real-world regression study. It is used here purely so every step of the calculation could be checked by hand.
